note: `overrides` had no source in Elixir in this lane, and Elixir has TWO constructs that produce it. `@impl` is Elixir's `@Override`: it asserts the next definition IS the implementation of a contract callback, and the compiler warns when the claim is false — so `overrides <Module.fn/arity> -> <Contract>.fn` is a member-level statement, the shape csharp and java publish for the same annotation. The CONTRACT is resolved in a fixed order and anything unresolvable stays SILENT: `@impl SomeProtocol` names it, an enclosing `defimpl` names it, exactly one `@behaviour` target names it, and several targets are narrowed by a `@callback` this module declares. Three silences are pinned because each is a place a coin toss could have been published as a fact: `@impl false` denies the implementation, `@impl true` with no nameable contract publishes nothing (`OntoUnnamed`), and a behaviour member with no `@impl` is not an override. `defoverridable` is the second construct: it publishes a function as replaceable and a later same-module definition of the same name AND arity replaces it, with the prior line on the edge (bash's `overridesLine` shape). A name the `defoverridable` did not list is not an override, and a `defp` is never one.

forbidRelationships.note: @impl true with no nameable contract must stay SILENT, not pick a contract
a behaviour member with no @impl is not an override
a defp is never an override
